0.title: Nahum: A Stronghold in the Day of Trouble
0.overview:
Nahum is a hard book, and it is meant to be. Three chapters, one subject: the fall of Nineveh, capital of the Assyrian empire. There is no call to repent in it and no appeal to Nineveh. It is an announcement, delivered to the people Assyria had been crushing, that the crushing is going to stop.

We know nothing about the prophet beyond his name and town, Nahum of Elkosh (1:1). He speaks of the sack of Thebes (663 BC) as past and foretells the fall of Nineveh (612 BC), so he preached in between, while Assyria still looked invincible.

Assyria's kings recorded their own atrocities with pride: cities burned, prisoners flayed, heads stacked in piles, whole populations deported. Assyria had destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC and besieged Jerusalem in 701. Read the book alongside Jonah: more than a century earlier Nineveh repented and was spared, but a later generation returned to the old violence. Repentance is not inherited.

The book falls into three parts. Chapter 1 is about God himself, jealous, avenging, slow to anger, with the line that holds the book together: The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble (1:7). Chapter 2 is the attack, written like a war report from inside the city: chariots racing, gates opening, treasure changing hands, and the taunt, Where is the lions' den? Chapter 3 is the indictment and the end: Woe to the bloody city, a power that seduced nations before it conquered them, whose wound at last cannot be healed.

Many readers find the violence of Nahum difficult, so three things need saying plainly.

First, God's anger here is an expression of his goodness. A God who could watch what Assyria did and feel nothing would not be loving; he would be indifferent. Nahum sets his fiercest verses beside The LORD is good, and means both.

Second, vengeance belongs to God, which means it does not belong to us: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). This book is not a licence for hatred; it is the reason hatred is unnecessary.

Third, the book quotes the creed of Exodus 34: God is slow to anger but will by no means clear the guilty. Jonah quoted the mercy half and resented it; Nahum quotes the justice half. At the cross God did not clear the guilty by pretending; he bore the guilt himself, so that his people are saved by him from the wrath of God (Rom 5:9).

That is why a verse from this fierce little book ends up preaching the gospel. The runner on the hills who publishes peace (1:15) is echoed by Isaiah (Isa 52:7) and applied by Paul to gospel preachers: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news! (Rom 10:15). One tyrant's fall set a runner going over the hills; the message Christians carry is that sin and death themselves have been beaten.

So Nahum speaks to anyone who has wondered whether cruelty simply wins. God keeps accounts, no empire is permanent, and the safest place in a violent world is in the hands of the God who knows those who take refuge in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A Jealous and Avenging God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD is a jealous and avenging God, yet slow to anger, and creation withers before him (vv. 1-6). Then the turn: The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The same God is a consuming fire to his enemies and a stronghold to those who take refuge in him.

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum of Elkosh. The LORD is a jealous and avenging God; the LORD is avenging and wrathful; the LORD takes vengeance on his adversaries and keeps wrath for his enemies. The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, and the LORD will by no means clear the guilty. His way is in whirlwind and storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know nothing about Nahum of Elkosh except these words. This is an oracle concerning Nineveh, the same city that had repented at Jonah's preaching more than a century before and been spared. A later generation has gone back to the old violence, and the reprieve has run out. Every generation must come to God for itself.

Jealous here is not petty envy. It is the jealousy of a husband whose wife is being taken from him, or of a father watching his children abused. A God who felt nothing about evil would not be good; he would be indifferent.

Avenging means that God settles accounts. Three times in one verse: avenging, avenging, takes vengeance. To a small nation that had watched the Assyrians flay prisoners alive and deport whole populations, this was not a frightening doctrine. It was the only hope of justice they had.

And it remains so. The alternative to God's vengeance is not a gentler world; it is a world where the torturer dies comfortably in old age and nothing is ever put right. Because God repays, his people never have to: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19).

Nahum is quoting the words God spoke about himself to Moses: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger ... but who will by no means clear the guilty (Exod 34:6-7). Jonah quoted the first half of that creed when he complained that God was too merciful (Jonah 4:2). Nahum quotes the second half.

Both halves are true, and they are held together in one sentence here: slow to anger and will by no means clear the guilty. God's patience is real; Nineveh had already had more than a century of it. But patience is not the same as pretending, and there comes a day when the account is settled.

The Christian knows where those two truths meet. At the cross God did not clear the guilty by ignoring guilt; he bore it himself, so that we are saved by him from the wrath of God (Rom 5:9).
verseByVerse.note: Nahum (“comfort”) foretells the fall of Nineveh, Assyria’s capital, which fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC — more than a century after Jonah’s preaching there.

verseByVerse.quote: He rebukes the sea and makes it dry; he dries up all the rivers; Bashan and Carmel wither; the bloom of Lebanon withers. The mountains quake before him; the hills melt; the earth heaves before him, the world and all who dwell in it. Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the heat of his anger? His wrath is poured out like fire, and the rocks are broken into pieces by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The picture is of the whole created order reacting to God's approach. He rebukes the sea, as he did at the Red Sea. Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon were the greenest, most fertile places the Israelites knew, and they wither like cut flowers.

Assyria was the strongest power on earth, and Nahum begins by showing that the mountains themselves cannot stand up to God. Empires are not in a different category.

Two questions, and both expect the answer "no one". Who can stand? Not Nineveh, with its walls; not anyone. If the rocks are broken into pieces, what hope has flesh and blood? It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb 10:31).
verseByVerse.note: Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon were the most fertile regions of the land.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him. But with an overflowing flood he will make a complete end of the adversaries, and will pursue his enemies into darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the storm comes one of the loveliest verses in the prophets, placed exactly where it is needed, right after the question Who can stand?

The LORD is good. The God of verses 2-6 is not merely powerful; he is good, and his goodness is the reason for his anger at cruelty.

A stronghold in the day of trouble. Nineveh trusted in its walls. God's people have a fortress that is a person. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble (Ps 46:1); The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed (Ps 9:9).

He knows those who take refuge in him. Not "he knows about them": he knows them, personally, by name. In a world where whole populations were being deported and counted as numbers, God knows the individuals who run to him.

What makes the difference between verse 6 and verse 7? It is not that some people are strong enough to stand; nobody is. It is refuge. The same God is a fire to those who defy him and a fortress to those who hide in him, and the only question is which side of the wall we are on.

The overflowing flood will make a complete end (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads "of her place"). The flood may be picture language for an overwhelming army; many also see in it the part the river is said to have played when the city fell (2:6). Either way, God's word proved true.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who plot against the LORD will be consumed (vv. 9-11). God will break the oppressor's yoke and cut off Nineveh's name (vv. 12-14), and a runner brings good news (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: When God deals with the oppressor, the news of it comes to his people as good news and peace.

verseByVerse.quote: What do you plot against the LORD? He will make a complete end; trouble will not rise up a second time. For they are like entangled thorns, like drunkards as they drink; they are consumed like stubble fully dried. From you came one who plotted evil against the LORD, a worthless counselor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question is almost pitying. What do you plot against the LORD? What exactly do you imagine you are going to do? Assyria had a strategy for every nation on the map, and no strategy at all for the God of heaven.

Trouble will not rise up a second time: when God deals with this enemy, it will not need doing again. He does not leave his work half finished.

Three pictures of how quickly it ends: entangled thorns that catch fire in a moment, drunkards too fuddled to defend themselves, stubble fully dried that flares and is gone.

Out of Nineveh came one who plotted evil against the LORD. Judah had met such men: the Assyrian officer who stood outside Jerusalem and mocked their God, and the king who sent him (2 Kgs 18:28-35; 19:22). Empires always produce advisers who think God is one more factor to be managed.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, "Though they are at full strength and many, they will be cut down and pass away. Though I have afflicted you, I will afflict you no more. And now I will break his yoke from off you and will burst your bonds apart." The LORD has given commandment about you: "No more shall your name be perpetuated; from the house of your gods I will cut off the carved image and the metal image. I will make your grave, for you are vile." Behold, upon the mountains, the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, O Judah; fulfill your vows, for never again shall the worthless pass through you; he is utterly cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns to speak to his own people, and every phrase is comfort. The enemy is at full strength, which is exactly how it looks from underneath, and it will still be cut down.

Then a sentence that only makes sense if God is sovereign over history: Though I have afflicted you, I will afflict you no more. God owns the affliction. Assyria was the rod in his hand for the discipline of his people. And when the discipline has done its work, he snaps the rod: I will break his yoke from off you.

Back to Nineveh, and the sentence is total: no descendants to carry the name, no gods left standing in the temple, only a grave. Assyrian kings spent fortunes building their names into stone. God says, I will make your grave.

(In the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 2, as the ESV notes.) Picture a watchman on Jerusalem's wall. Far off on the hills a runner appears, and as he comes the watchman can see that he is running like a man with good news. The message is that the enemy has fallen.

Isaiah used the same words about a greater message: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace ... who says to Zion, "Your God reigns" (Isa 52:7). And Paul took them and applied them to gospel preachers: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news! (Rom 10:15).

That is the line that runs from Nahum to us. Nineveh's fall was good news because an oppressor was finished. The gospel is better news of the same kind: sin, death and the devil have been defeated by Christ, and messengers are still running over the hills to say so.

And see the response God asks for: Keep your feasts, O Judah; fulfill your vows. Worship, and keep your promises. When God deals with what we feared, the right answer is not merely relief but praise.

1.title: The LORD Is Good, a Stronghold
1.overview: The LORD is a jealous and avenging God, slow to anger yet one who will by no means clear the guilty, and no part of creation can stand before him (vv. 1-6). But the LORD is good, a stronghold for those who take refuge in him (vv. 7-8). Nineveh's plotting will burn like stubble; God will break the yoke from his people, and a runner on the mountains brings the news of peace (vv. 9-15).
1.theology:
God's jealousy and vengeance are expressions of his goodness; a God indifferent to cruelty would not be good (vv. 2-3; Rom 12:19).

God is both slow to anger and certain to judge; his patience is not indifference (v. 3; Exod 34:6-7; Jonah 4:2).

No power in creation can stand before God, and empires are no exception (vv. 4-6; Heb 10:31).

The same God is a fire to his enemies and a stronghold to those who take refuge in him, and he knows them personally (v. 7; Ps 46:1; 9:9).

God rules the affliction of his own people and ends it when its work is done (vv. 12-13).

The fall of an oppressor is good news, and the gospel is the greater good news of the same kind (v. 15; Isa 52:7; Rom 10:15).

Deliverance calls for worship and kept promises, not just relief (v. 15).
1.examples:
A city that repented in Jonah's day and forgot it in its grandchildren's.

Green Lebanon withering like cut flowers at God's approach.

Two questions nobody can answer: who can stand, who can endure?

A fortress that is not a wall but a person.

An empire with a plan for every nation and none for God.

Dry stubble catching light in an instant.

A runner on the hills whose gait says the war is over.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The scatterer has come up against you, for the LORD is restoring the majesty of Jacob (vv. 1-2). Chariots race through the streets, the river gates open, and the city is plundered and left desolate (vv. 3-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The empire that scattered the nations is scattered, and God does it for the sake of his own people.

verseByVerse.quote: The scatterer has come up against you. Man the ramparts; watch the road; dress for battle; collect all your strength. For the LORD is restoring the majesty of Jacob as the majesty of Israel, for plunderers have plundered them and ruined their branches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nahum turns to the city and speaks as if the siege has begun. The scatterer is the invading force, and there is bitter justice in the title: Assyria had scattered nation after nation, deporting whole peoples, and now someone has come to scatter her.

The commands come like a sergeant's orders: Man the ramparts; watch the road; dress for battle (the ESV notes the Hebrew is "gird your loins", tucking up the long robe to fight), collect all your strength. It will not be enough.

Here is the reason behind the noise: the LORD is restoring the majesty of Jacob. God is not merely demolishing an empire; he is rebuilding a people whose branches had been stripped bare. Israel is often pictured as a vine that God planted (Ps 80:8), and this vine has been hacked back to the stump.

The word restoring matters. God's work is not only to remove what hurt his people but to give back what was lost, as he promised through Joel: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten (Joel 2:25). Behind the rise and fall of superpowers is God's care for his own, and his intention to make them flourish again.

verseByVerse.quote: The shield of his mighty men is red; his soldiers are clothed in scarlet. The chariots come with flashing metal on the day he musters them; the cypress spears are brandished. The chariots race madly through the streets; they rush to and fro through the squares; they gleam like torches; they dart like lightning. He remembers his officers; they stumble as they go, they hasten to the wall; the siege tower is set up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nahum writes like a war reporter. Shields red, uniforms scarlet, metal flashing, spears brandished. Then the chariots are inside: racing madly through the streets, gleaming like torches, darting like lightning. The short phrases give the sense of a city collapsing faster than anyone can think.

Inside, the Assyrian king calls up his best men, and they are useless: they stumble as they go. Outside, the siege tower is already in place (the ESV notes this may be a "mantelet", a screen to protect attackers at the wall). The defence is a shambles while the attack is methodical.

verseByVerse.quote: The river gates are opened; the palace melts away; its mistress is stripped; she is carried off, her slave girls lamenting, moaning like doves and beating their breasts. Nineveh is like a pool whose waters run away. "Halt! Halt!" they cry, but none turns back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city stood where two rivers met, and its defences depended on them. The river gates are opened, and the water that protected Nineveh becomes the way in. Ancient writers record that a flood broke part of the wall in the final siege. Whatever exactly happened, the prophet's words came true.

And the palace melts away, a phrase that describes both a building and a government losing its nerve.

Nineveh's queen, or perhaps the city pictured as a woman, is led away (the ESV notes that the word rendered its mistress is uncertain, and that stripped may be "exiled"). Her women go with her, moaning like doves. For a hundred years Assyrian soldiers had marched other people's daughters away in exactly this manner.

Nineveh like a pool is a brilliant image (the ESV notes the Hebrew here is uncertain). The city had been a reservoir, gathering the wealth and people of the world into itself. Now the dam is broken and it all runs out. Officers shout Halt! Halt! and nobody stops. Authority has evaporated, and that is what the end of an empire looks like from inside.
verseByVerse.note: The “river gates” may refer to Nineveh’s canals and floodgates.

verseByVerse.quote: Plunder the silver, plunder the gold! There is no end of the treasure or of the wealth of all precious things. Desolate! Desolation and ruin! Hearts melt and knees tremble; anguish is in all loins; all faces grow pale!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The invaders are invited to help themselves, and the treasure is no end: the accumulated loot of the ancient world, gathered by a century of conquest. It changes hands in a day.

Everything Nineveh took from others is taken from Nineveh. The wealth of an unjust empire is never really its own; it is on loan until the reckoning.

The three exclamations of verse 10 hammer down like blows. Then the effects, catalogued body by body: hearts, knees, bodies, faces. This is what terror looks like, and it is the terror Assyria had inflicted on others for generations, now experienced at home.

A Christian reads this with two responses at once. There is relief that cruelty is stopped, and there is sober fear, because what happened to Nineveh is a small picture of the last day. The right answer to both is to run to the stronghold of 1:7 while the door is open.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where is the lions' den? (vv. 11-12). Behold, I am against you, declares the LORD of hosts (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Predatory power looks permanent until God says he is against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Where is the lions' den, the feeding place of the young lions, where the lion and lioness went, where his cubs were, with none to disturb? The lion tore enough for his cubs and strangled prey for his lionesses; he filled his caves with prey and his dens with torn flesh. Behold, I am against you, declares the LORD of hosts, and I will burn your chariots in smoke, and the sword shall devour your young lions. I will cut off your prey from the earth, and the voice of your messengers shall no longer be heard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now comes a taunt song, and it is perfectly aimed. Assyrian kings loved the lion: they hunted lions, and their palace walls were carved with lion hunts. Nahum takes their favourite symbol and turns it into an indictment.

Look at what the lion did. He tore and strangled prey and filled his dens with torn flesh, and he did it for his cubs and his lionesses. That is exactly how empires justify plunder: we are providing for our own. The prosperity at home was paid for by the killing abroad.

Now the question is simply, Where is the lions' den? It is gone. Ask the same question of any number of regimes that seemed unanswerable in their day.

Here is the sentence that settles everything: Behold, I am against you, declares the LORD of hosts. Not "your enemies are against you", which Assyria could handle. God is. (The ESV notes the Hebrew reads "her" for your.)

The voice of your messengers is a pointed ending. Assyrian envoys had stood outside Jerusalem's walls shouting threats and mocking the living God. That voice would be heard no more. Nineveh fell in 612 BC to an alliance of Babylonians and Medes, and was so thoroughly lost that later travellers walked over the mound without knowing a city lay beneath.

For a believer under a boot, this is the comfort of the chapter: the day comes when God says, I am against you, and the lions' den is empty.

And there is a greater lion hunt in the Bible than any carved on an Assyrian wall. At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them (Col 2:15), and at the end he rides out as the one called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war (Rev 19:11). Every empire that devours people is living on borrowed time, because the Lord of hosts has already won the decisive battle.

2.title: Where Is the Lions' Den?
2.overview:
Nahum describes Nineveh's fall as if from inside the city: the attackers' red shields and racing chariots, the river gates opened, the palace melting away, the people running out like water and the plunder carried off (vv. 1-10). Behind it all the LORD is restoring the majesty of Jacob (v. 2).

Where now is the lions' den, where the lion tore prey for his cubs and filled his caves with torn flesh? The LORD of hosts declares he is against her: her chariots will burn, her young lions fall by the sword, her prey be cut off, and the voice of her messengers heard no more (vv. 11-13).
2.theology:
God repays in kind: the scatterer of nations is scattered (v. 1).

Behind the fall of empires lies God's care for his own people (v. 2).

Human defences fail exactly where they were trusted most (vv. 5-6).

Wealth built on injustice is held only until the reckoning (v. 9).

The terror an aggressor inflicts eventually comes home (v. 10).

Predatory power provides for its own by destroying others, and God names it for what it is (vv. 11-12).

Nothing survives the sentence "I am against you, declares the LORD of hosts" (v. 13).
2.examples:
Orders shouted on a wall that is already lost.

Chariots darting like lightning through the squares.

The river that protected a city becoming the way in.

Officers crying "Halt!" while everyone runs.

A century of plunder changing hands in a day.

A carved lion hunt on a palace wall, and an empty den.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Woe to the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder— no end to the prey!<sup>2</sup>The crack of the whip, and rumble of the wheel, galloping horse and bounding chariot!<sup>3</sup>Horsemen charging, flashing sword and glittering spear, hosts of slain, heaps of corpses, dead bodies without end— they stumble over the bodies!<sup>4</sup>And all for the countless whorings of the prostitute, graceful and of deadly charms, who betrays nations with her whorings, and peoples with her charms.<sup>5</sup>Behold, I am against you, declares the LORD of hosts, and will lift up your skirts over your face; and I will make nations look at your nakedness and kingdoms at your shame.<sup>6</sup>I will throw filth at you and treat you with contempt and make you a spectacle.<sup>7</sup>And all who look at you will shrink from you and say, "Wasted is Nineveh; who will grieve for her?" Where shall I seek comforters for you?<sup>8</sup>Are you better than Thebes that sat by the Nile, with water around her, her rampart a sea, and water her wall?<sup>9</sup>Cush was her strength; Egypt too, and that without limit; Put and the Libyans were her helpers.<sup>10</sup>Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity; her infants were dashed in pieces at the head of every street; for her honored men lots were cast, and all her great men were bound in chains.<sup>11</sup>You also will be drunken; you will go into hiding; you will seek a refuge from the enemy.<sup>12</sup>All your fortresses are like fig trees with first-ripe figs— if shaken they fall into the mouth of the eater.<sup>13</sup>Behold, your troops are women in your midst. The gates of your land are wide open to your enemies; fire has devoured your bars.<sup>14</sup>Draw water for the siege; strengthen your forts; go into the clay; tread the mortar; take hold of the brick mold!<sup>15</sup>There will the fire devour you; the sword will cut you off. It will devour you like the locust. Multiply yourselves like the locust; multiply like the grasshopper!<sup>16</sup>You increased your merchants more than the stars of the heavens. The locust spreads its wings and flies away.<sup>17</sup>Your princes are like grasshoppers, your scribes like clouds of locusts settling on the fences in a day of cold— when the sun rises, they fly away; no one knows where they are.<sup>18</sup>Your shepherds are asleep, O king of Assyria; your nobles slumber. Your people are scattered on the mountains with none to gather them.<sup>19</sup>There is no easing your hurt; your wound is grievous. All who hear the news about you clap their hands over you. For upon whom has not come your unceasing evil?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder (v. 1): war, corpses and seduction (vv. 2-4). Behold, I am against you, and no one will grieve for her (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: God exposes the true character of a power that lived by terror and deceit, and no one mourns its passing.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder— no end to the prey! The crack of the whip, and rumble of the wheel, galloping horse and bounding chariot! Horsemen charging, flashing sword and glittering spear, hosts of slain, heaps of corpses, dead bodies without end— they stumble over the bodies! And all for the countless whorings of the prostitute, graceful and of deadly charms, who betrays nations with her whorings, and peoples with her charms.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three charges in one line. Bloody: Assyrian kings boasted in their own inscriptions of flaying prisoners and stacking heads. Full of lies: their diplomacy was a machine of broken promises. Plunder: the economy ran on other people's property.

The word Woe is the cry at a funeral. God is announcing a death.

Nahum writes almost without verbs, in a rush of sounds and sights: The crack of the whip, and rumble of the wheel, hooves, swords, spears. Then the sentence stops on what all the glamour of war actually produces: heaps of corpses, dead bodies without end, and soldiers who stumble over the bodies.

The Bible never romanticises war: it lets us hear the noise, and then it shows us the bodies.

Why did it happen? And all for the countless whorings of the prostitute. Nineveh is pictured as a woman who is graceful and of deadly charms. Empires do not only conquer; they seduce. Assyria offered trade, protection and a share in the glory, and nation after nation signed up and was ruined.

Revelation uses the same image for the world system that seduces the nations away from God, the great prostitute with whom the kings of the earth commit immorality (Rev 17:1-2). Every age has a version: a power that promises security and prosperity if you will just accept its terms and its gods.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am against you, declares the LORD of hosts, and will lift up your skirts over your face; and I will make nations look at your nakedness and kingdoms at your shame. I will throw filth at you and treat you with contempt and make you a spectacle. And all who look at you will shrink from you and say, "Wasted is Nineveh; who will grieve for her?" Where shall I seek comforters for you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The image is deliberately shocking: the punishment of a prostitute in the ancient world, publicly stripped and shamed. It is hard to read, and it is meant to be. What Nineveh had done to others, in the most humiliating ways, is now done to her in front of the watching nations.

A note of care is needed here. This is God's sentence on a violent empire, not a licence for anyone to treat women, or anyone else, with contempt. The picture works precisely because such treatment is shameful, and God is saying that Assyria's public reputation will end in shame as complete as the shame she inflicted.

The loneliest question in the book is who will grieve for her? A city that ruled the world will not have a single mourner. God asks, almost ironically, Where shall I seek comforters for you? and no answer comes.

Power built on fear leaves no friends behind it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–19 — Are You Better Than Thebes?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Are you better than Thebes? (vv. 8-10). Her fortresses fall, her preparations fail, her officials fly away like locusts, and the world claps its hands (vv. 11-19).
verseByVerse.theology: No defences, alliances or wealth can save a nation whose cruelty has caught up with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you better than Thebes that sat by the Nile, with water around her, her rampart a sea, and water her wall? Cush was her strength; Egypt too, and that without limit; Put and the Libyans were her helpers. Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity; her infants were dashed in pieces at the head of every street; for her honored men lots were cast, and all her great men were bound in chains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nahum's strongest card is a memory. Thebes (the ESV notes the Hebrew name is No-amon) was the ancient capital of Upper Egypt, protected by the Nile, backed by Cush and Egypt, with Put and the Libyans as allies. It looked untouchable.

And Assyria had destroyed it, in 663 BC, within living memory of Nahum's hearers. So the question lands with full weight: Are you better than Thebes? You proved that walls of water and a ring of allies count for nothing. Why should your own walls be different?

Verse 10 lists what Assyrian conquest looked like, without relish: it is evidence, and Nineveh's own soldiers had done it.

What we do to others has a way of describing what will be done to us. That is not karma, an impersonal force; it is the judgment of a God who keeps accounts.

How can a good God bring such a fall on a whole city, children included? Scripture does not hide the cost. Judgment in history falls on whole communities, as the consequences of sin always do, and Nineveh had had more than a century of patience since Jonah's day. The same God had once said of this city's people and little ones, should not I pity Nineveh (Jonah 4:11), and he has not changed; he has no pleasure in the death of anyone (Ezek 18:32). The Judge of all the earth will do what is right with every child (Gen 18:25), and many Christians, with the Westminster Confession of Faith (10.3), take comfort that little ones who die are not beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Thebes (No-amon), Egypt’s great city on the Nile, fell to Assyria in 663 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: You also will be drunken; you will go into hiding; you will seek a refuge from the enemy. All your fortresses are like fig trees with first-ripe figs— if shaken they fall into the mouth of the eater. Behold, your troops are women in your midst. The gates of your land are wide open to your enemies; fire has devoured your bars. Draw water for the siege; strengthen your forts; go into the clay; tread the mortar; take hold of the brick mold! There will the fire devour you; the sword will cut you off. It will devour you like the locust. Multiply yourselves like the locust; multiply like the grasshopper!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two words in the first line matter. Drunken is the prophets' picture of a nation staggering under the cup of God's wrath; Jeremiah was told to make the nations drink, be drunk and vomit, fall and rise no more (Jer 25:27). And you will seek a refuge: Nineveh will go looking for the very thing Judah already had, for The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble (1:7). The tragedy of the book is not that God had no refuge to offer, but that this city never wanted it.

The famous Assyrian border fortresses are fig trees with first-ripe figs: give the trunk one shake and the fruit drops straight into the mouth of whoever is standing underneath. Defences that took generations to build will be lost in a moment.

The taunt your troops are women belongs to the rough speech of ancient warfare; the point is that the terror of the world has lost its nerve. The gates stand open and the iron bars are burned.

God tells them to prepare: store water, repair walls, mix clay, make bricks. It sounds like practical advice, and it is bitter irony. There will the fire devour you. Work all night on the walls if you like; the outcome is fixed.

Effort cannot compensate for being on the wrong side of God; the only safety is the refuge of 1:7.

verseByVerse.quote: You increased your merchants more than the stars of the heavens. The locust spreads its wings and flies away. Your princes are like grasshoppers, your scribes like clouds of locusts settling on the fences in a day of cold— when the sun rises, they fly away; no one knows where they are. Your shepherds are asleep, O king of Assyria; your nobles slumber. Your people are scattered on the mountains with none to gather them. There is no easing your hurt; your wound is grievous. All who hear the news about you clap their hands over you. For upon whom has not come your unceasing evil?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nineveh's wealth came through a swarm of merchants, and its government ran on a swarm of officials (the ESV notes princes may be "guards" and scribes "marshals"). Locusts are the perfect image: they strip a land bare, and then, the moment the weather turns, they are gone. When the sun rises, they fly away; no one knows where they are.

Every institution built on people who are there for what they can get discovers this on the day of trouble. The crowd that feeds on success is not the crowd that stands by you in failure.

The leaders are asleep, which in the Bible's language means both careless and dead. And the people are scattered on the mountains with none to gather them. That phrase is used elsewhere for sheep without a shepherd, and it is the saddest line in the chapter, because the ordinary people of Nineveh are its final victims.

And the phrase reaches forward. Israel's own shepherds slept too (Ezek 34), until God said he would come and shepherd the sheep himself. When Jesus saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matt 9:36). Nineveh's people were scattered with none to gather them; the Shepherd who does gather, and who will neither slumber nor sleep (Ps 121:4), is the answer this chapter leaves us longing for.

The book ends with a wound that will not heal and a world that applauds. All who hear the news about you clap their hands, and the last line explains why: upon whom has not come your unceasing evil? Everybody had suffered from Assyria. Nobody is sorry.

How should a Christian feel reading this? Not gloating; Scripture forbids rejoicing when an enemy falls (Prov 24:17). But relief at the end of cruelty is right, and heaven itself rejoices when a tyrant system falls: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her! (Rev 18:20).

Everything in these three chapters came true, and the God who brought this city down is the same God who is called, in the middle of chapter 1, a stronghold in the day of trouble. Nineveh and Judah did not meet two different Gods. The difference was that one hid from him and the other hid in him. That refuge now has a name, and his arms were opened on a cross.

3.title: Woe to the Bloody City
3.overview: Woe to the bloody city, full of lies and plunder, whose charging horsemen leave heaps of corpses, and who seduces nations like a prostitute (vv. 1-4). The LORD will expose her shame, and no one will grieve for her (vv. 5-7). She is no better than Thebes, whom she herself destroyed; her fortresses will drop like ripe figs, and all her preparations for siege will not save her (vv. 8-15). Her merchants and officials vanish like locusts, her people are scattered with none to gather them, and all who hear the news clap their hands (vv. 16-19).
3.theology:
God names violence, deceit and plunder for what they are, and announces a funeral over them (v. 1).

Scripture does not romanticise war; it shows the corpses (vv. 2-3).

Empires seduce as well as conquer, and the same picture is later used of the world system opposed to God (v. 4; Rev 17:1-2).

Power built on fear dies unmourned (v. 7).

What a nation does to others describes what will be done to it, because God keeps accounts (vv. 8-10).

Preparation and effort cannot save those who are on the wrong side of God (vv. 14-15).

People who attach themselves to success leave when the weather changes (vv. 16-17).

Relief at the end of cruelty is right, and gloating is not; heaven rejoices at justice done (v. 19; Prov 24:17; Rev 18:20).
3.examples:
A funeral cry raised over a living empire.

Whips, wheels and glittering spears, and then the bodies underfoot.

A power that seduces nations before it conquers them.

A world capital with no one left to mourn it.

A city with a river for a wall, already destroyed by the questioner.

Fortresses like fig trees, dropping their fruit at one shake.

Officials like locusts, gone the moment the sun comes up.
